newsitem.title: USA: Boeing to slow job growth rate.
newsitem.headline: Boeing to slow job growth rate.

text.p: Boeing Co President and Chief Executive Officer Phil Condit said at a news briefing the company will continue expanding its workforce next year, but at a slower rate than in 1996.

So far this year, the company has added nearly 20,000 employees to its total workforce of about 125,000, which does not include 21,000 employees added through the acquisition last week of Rockwell International Corp's defense and space businesses.
Condit declined to predict how many jobs Boeing might add next year, saying the company planned to issue its annual employment forecast next month.
Condit said the year just ended had been "absolutely fantastic," noting that Boeing has announced orders for a record 621 jets this year, up from 326 last year.

Despite the rapid increase, Condit said the order rate is only one-third of the peak years of the 1980s when adjusted for the size of the world's jet fleet, raising hope that the current business cycle might not end in the type of severe situation that hit the industry in the early 1990s.
"I have some significant hope that this business cycle may not be as dramatically up and down," Condit said.
"As we look at the ordering patterns so far, they are still very much lower than we saw in the last cycle, and I think there's a good chance that we can extend that over a longer period," he said.

He said the business would remain cyclical, but because of cost-cutting efforts he said Boeing might be able to avoid repeating the kind of deep job cuts it was forced to make over the past several years.

Condit declined to comment on a published report that British Airways Plc had shelved plans to be a launch customer for the proposed stretch version of the 747 jumbo jet, intended for initial delivery in 2001.
But he said he was not aware of any change in the carrier's interest in the model.
Condit said he thought there was a 50-50 chance Boeing would launch the planned jet in the next six months.
Condit said he expected the order strength to continue next year and to be geographically balanced.
Condit said he also expected China to resume ordering Boeing jets next year after a long break largely blamed on politics.
He also said he expected a pickup in orders from Japan and Europe as well as additional U.S. orders.
